newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin heart operation starts in Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin heart operation starts in Moscow.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's long-awaited heart surgery began in Moscow early on Tuesday, a presidential spokesman said.

Before entering the operating theatre, Yeltsin signed a decree handing over his presidential powers, including control of Russia's nuclear arsenal, to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Itar-Tass news agency said.
If all goes according to plan, the president will resume his authority shortly after he emerges from the anaesthetic.

Yeltsin, 65, was driven early on Tuesday in a motorcade from the Barvikha sanatorium west of the Russian capital to the Moscow Cardiology Centre where the triple or quadruple bypass was being carried out.
Security was tight around the hospital, a collection of whitewashed buildings in woodland near the city's motorway ring.
The operation, due to last several hours, was to be performed by a team headed by Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin, advised by U.S. heart surgery pioneer Michael DeBakey and others.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky called a press briefing for 10 a.m. (0700 GMT).

Yeltsin, who has suffered from heart problems for years, was re-elected to a second four-year term in July. He announced in September he had decided to undergo surgery and spent six weeks preparing for the operation.

The operation coincides with planned trade union strikes and protests in Moscow and elsewhere across Russia against delayed wages -- one of the biggest social and economic problems facing the country.
It also coincides with the U.S. presidential election, which will take the world news spotlight away from Moscow for at least 24 hours.

Yeltsin's long illness, which has removed him from the political front line since just before his victory in the presidential election, has encouraged Kremlin infighting and uncertainty over who is making decisions.

Chernomyrdin, standing in for Yeltsin, has been trying to project an atmosphere of business as usual but uncertainty has been stimulated by the Kremlin's reticence over the timing and details of Yeltsin's operation.
By the standards of the Soviet Union, Moscow has shown unprecedented candour but by modern U.S. standards it has given out very little medical information.

A medical bulletin released on Monday said Yeltsin's blood pressure, temperature and pulse were normal but gave no other details except to say his current condition showed "all organs and systems to be functioning at an optimal level".
"This makes it possible to undertake the operation with a high level of certainty and confidence," the doctors said.
